title: Early songs and Moonlight Mexico
summary: Levy tells of writing 35th Street and other songs, losing an uncopyrighted foxtrot, and his Moonlight Mexico record released as rock and roll arrived.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: And then I wrote, then I had three little girls and I said, well, maybe I said try to write something, make some money. So, well, in the 20, I think 1920 and 21 I wrote that 35th Street. And I had written Skizics. You know the little Skizics in front of the paper? Yes. Or the cuter song Skizic. I remember it too. And I took it downtown and they kept it for about a year. I forget the publisher. They kept it for about a year and did nothing with it. And then I wrote another, I wrote another little Foxtrot and I carried it to a publisher. I forgot to copyright it and I was such a hurry to get down with it. I was so inspired with it. And they lost it, they said, and I never heard nothing more about that. So from then on, as soon as I wrote something, I got it copyrighted there. And so, in this writing, I had three wonderful little girls and they were wonderful children. They weren't bad at all, they were wonderful kids and they inspired me. So, I want to tell you, I'm going to jump ahead of myself to tell you about Fraternity Records. They recorded my Moonlight Mexico, which was a Spanish 3-4, totally different from anything I'd ever written. And Dick Noel of NBC's Breakfast Club, he recorded, this was about two years ago, and they recorded in Hollywood with Norman Luboff's Choir Byers. A beautiful record. I'm sorry I have, I think maybe I might have it on the tape there. And the rock and roll was in, and nobody bought the song.
Well, sometimes, yeah, sometimes those things are slow starters. Yes. I mean, they're always for a period.
Well, it just, it came out just about when everybody, the rock and roll, the kids.
